text:
You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure for this public goods game, where keeping tokens in my own account benefits me directly but imposes a small cost on others, while contributing to the group account gives everyone a smaller shared return—so I'm calculating how my choice of k versus g affects my total points given the fixed 18-point base and the four-member split.

The math shows that each kept token nets +0.1 to total group welfare (gaining me 1, costing others 0.9 combined), while each contributed token nets +0.3 to total welfare but only returns 0.3 to me personally. So socially the group is better off if everyone contributes everything, yet individually keeping tokens is still the dominant strategy since my personal return from keeping (1) beats my personal return from contributing (0.3)—this is the classic free-rider tension in public goods games.

If everyone keeps all 20 each round, each person nets 20 per round; if everyone fully cooperates, each nets 42 per round, a huge gap. Given this is a repeated 10-round game against unknown others, I'm leaning toward starting with a generous contribution to signal cooperation and see how others respond.
